subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Cell and nuclear division
bigPicture: Cells come only from other cells. Before dividing, a cell copies its DNA; mitosis then gives two identical nuclei for growth and repair, while meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles alleles for sexual reproduction. HL adds how cyclins control the cycle and how faults in this control lead to cancer.

keyIdeas.answer: By division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells, in all living organisms.

keyIdeas.cue: How does cytokinesis differ in animal and plant cells?
keyIdeas.answer: Animal: a ring of contractile actin and myosin pinches the membrane inwards (cleavage furrow). Plant: vesicles gather at the equator and build a new membrane and cell wall (cell plate).

Usually, but not always. Oogenesis gives one large egg and small polar bodies; yeast budding gives a small bud. Each daughter must still get at least one mitochondrion and other organelles that only form by division.

keyIdeas.cue: What are the roles of mitosis and meiosis?
keyIdeas.answer: Nuclear division must happen before cell division so no cell lacks a nucleus. Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and genome the same. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates genetic diversity.

keyIdeas.cue: Why must DNA replicate before division?
keyIdeas.answer: So each chromosome has two identical chromatids, held together until anaphase, one going to each daughter nucleus.

keyIdeas.cue: What do mitosis and meiosis have in common?
keyIdeas.answer: Chromosomes condense by supercoiling around histones, so they can be moved without tangling. Microtubules (spindle) and motor proteins move them.

Prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane breaks down, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes line up on the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids separated to opposite poles), telophase (nuclear membranes re-form, chromosomes decondense). Result: two genetically identical nuclei.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you identify mitosis phases in micrographs?
keyIdeas.answer: Prophase: visible threads, no clear line. Metaphase: a line of chromosomes across the middle. Anaphase: two V-shaped groups moving apart. Telophase: two clusters at the poles, often with a forming cell plate or furrow.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is meiosis a reduction division?
keyIdeas.answer: A diploid nucleus (2n, two sets of chromosomes) gives four haploid nuclei (n). Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (first segregation); meiosis II separates sister chromatids (second segregation). It is needed so fertilisation restores, not doubles, the chromosome number.

keyIdeas.cue: How does non-disjunction cause Down syndrome?
keyIdeas.answer: Homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or chromatids (meiosis II) fail to separate, so a gamete has an extra chromosome 21. After fertilisation the zygote has three copies (trisomy 21). Risk increases with maternal age.
Crossing over in prophase I swaps sections between non-sister chromatids of homologues. Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I gives 2ⁿ combinations (2²³ in humans).
For growth (plant meristems, early embryos), routine cell replacement (skin) and repair (wound healing).

keyIdeas.cue: What are the phases of the cell cycle?
keyIdeas.answer: Interphase: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), then mitosis, then cytokinesis.
It is metabolically very active: the cell grows by making proteins, membranes and other components, copies its DNA, and increases its mitochondria (and chloroplasts) by their growth and division.

keyIdeas.cue: How do cyclins control the cell cycle?
keyIdeas.answer: Different cyclins rise and fall in concentration during the cycle. A specific cyclin must reach a threshold for the cell to pass each checkpoint. Names of specific cyclins aren't needed.

keyIdeas.cue: How do mutations cause uncontrolled division?
keyIdeas.answer: Proto-oncogenes (which promote division) can mutate into oncogenes, which are permanently 'on'. Tumour suppressor genes (which normally stop division) can be inactivated. Either way cells divide without control, forming a tumour.

keyIdeas.cue: Benign vs malignant tumours? What is the mitotic index?
keyIdeas.answer: Benign: grows slowly, stays in place, doesn't invade, not cancer. Malignant: divides fast, invades neighbouring tissue and can spread (metastasis) from a primary tumour to form secondary tumours: cancer. Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total cells; a high value suggests rapid division.

keyTerms.def: Division of the cytoplasm after nuclear division.
One set (n) / two sets (2n) of chromosomes.
A pair of homologous chromosomes joined in meiosis I.
Failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis.
Protein whose concentration controls progress through the cell cycle.
Spread of cancer cells to form secondary tumours.

workedExamples.title: Mitotic index
workedExamples.prompt: A micrograph of a tumour shows 240 cells; 36 are in mitosis. Normal tissue has an index of 0.05. Calculate and comment.
workedExamples.answer: 0.15: cells in the tumour are dividing much faster than normal.

workedExamples.title: Combinations from random orientation
workedExamples.prompt: How many chromosome combinations can a gamete have from random orientation alone in a species with 2n = 8?

misconceptions.right: DNA replicates in S phase of interphase.
It is the most metabolically active phase.
